doc.title: Vince Giordano interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2007

title: Studying the Schillinger Method with Bill Challis
summary: He sought out arranger Bill Challis in Massapequa, studied Schillinger on graph paper, and talks with Challis and Chauncey Morehouse in their later years.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Learning your horn: teachers, lessons and fees

blocks.x: Yeah. Tell me about the Schillinger Method with Bill Challis.

With Bill Challis, yeah. Well joining the union, I got the union directory. And I had been reading this book called “Jazz: the New York Scene” by Charters and Kunstadt. I love that book and it’s a wonderful book. And they mention Bill Challis a few times and I just happened to be flipping in the arranger section and I see William Challis in Massapequa, Long Island. I’m in Smithtown. And I wrote him a letter and I said I’d love to study with you. And he said fine. And my dad, again, takes me out there, because I’m still this teenager. And my dream with Bill Challis was to have a nice manuscript paper and some pencil and just start writing or start analyzing his work, whatever. But he stopped that right from the beginning. He says, “no, I want you to learn the Schillinger Method.” He said, “in the 1930s I was there with George Gershwin two rows over, and we had Glenn Miller, and so many musicians. They were studying this way of making their music fresh and they could per”— what’s the word here — I just lost the name of what we used to talk about — well we went through this stuff and it was about a year and a half. And I was still in high school and trying to do my grades and my gigs and we’d be there with graph paper and we really never got into the music. The best part of my sessions with Bill Challis was the two hours after where I used to talk with him. And sometimes the old drummer Chauncey Morehouse from the Jean Goldkette band was there and in fact one day I came about 15 minutes early and Chauncey was there and Bill and they were playing four hands at the piano, and they were trying to write a rock song called “Swamp Boogie.” And I was this young teenager and they said, “hey kid, what do you think about this?” And I said, “well guys I really don’t know much about Rock & Roll. Let’s talk about Frankie Trumbauer and Bix again.” But it was kind of sad because really time had
left, it had passed these fellows by. You know they just were looking for a gig and hoping to write a song, and that’s a long winded story about the Schillinger Method.
No I like to hear stuff like that. I mean how old would they have been at that time?
Were they still — after their heyday did they stay in music?

Well Chauncey played a little bit of bass drum in the Goldman concert band. His eyesight was pretty bad and he really wasn’t up to studio work anymore, his chops just weren’t there. Bill really wasn’t doing anything. He got an occasional call from Manhattan Transfer to write a few charts for them and he called me up and said, “I’ve got this young group they want me to recreate some Goldkette things. And I didn’t have the heart to tell him it wasn’t my arrangements, it was Don Murray’s arrangements, so I took the gig.” And you know Bill, pretty much after Eddie Fisher — he did all Eddie Fisher’s arrangements — he really wasn’t used anymore. Again, they just went for the younger folks and he just lived out there in Long Island with his sister and I guess had Social Security and that was it.
